title: Kaikeyi's two wishes
hook: the maid Manthara; the old promise called in

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita's swayamvara: a bow snapped, a garland placed. Your line was choose. What did you decide? Today, years later, back in Ayodhya, a happy announcement goes wrong overnight. Day thirty-nine.

Dasharatha is old now, and he makes the announcement the whole kingdom wants: tomorrow, Rama will be crowned as heir. The city goes wild. Flags, flowers, lamps in every window. And in the palace, Queen Kaikeyi, Bharata's mother, hears the news and is delighted. She loves Rama. She even gives a jewel to the servant who brought the news. That servant is her old maid, Manthara, who came with her from her childhood home. And Manthara throws the jewel down. Are you a fool, she says. When Rama is king, his mother will be queen mother, and you'll be her servant. And your son, Bharata, will have nothing.
screen: `TOMORROW, RAMA WILL BE CROWNED.` → `KAIKEYI IS DELIGHTED.` → `MANTHARA THROWS THE JEWEL DOWN.`

segments.voice: At first Kaikeyi argues. Rama is good. Rama is fair. But Manthara keeps talking, all night, and slowly the fear gets in. Then Manthara reminds her of something. Long ago, in a battle, Dasharatha was wounded, and Kaikeyi saved his life. In gratitude, he promised her two wishes, anything she asked, and she never used them. Use them now. So Kaikeyi goes to the room where a queen goes when she is angry, throws off her jewelry, and lies on the bare floor. Dasharatha finds her there, and he's frantic. What's wrong? I'll give you anything. And she makes him swear it, on Rama's name. Then she asks. First wish: crown Bharata instead. Second wish: send Rama into the forest, in exile, for fourteen years. The old king collapses. He begs. He argues. He pleads all night. But he gave his word, and a king's word is dharma. He can't take it back. Now, who is to blame? The tradition argues. In Valmiki, Kaikeyi and Manthara make a real, human choice. In some later tellings, the gods themselves arrange it: they send the goddess Saraswati to turn Manthara's mind, because Rama has to reach the forest to do what he was born to do. Those tellings are gentler on Kaikeyi. Strip the story down and it's simple. Two wishes, given in a grateful moment years ago, almost forgotten. Then someone picks them up, and they become a weapon. Words have weight. A promise keeps its weight long after the moment you made it.
screen: `MANTHARA TALKS ALL NIGHT.` · `THE OLD PROMISE: TWO WISHES.` · `CROWN BHARATA. EXILE RAMA.` · `WHO IS TO BLAME? IT DEPENDS.` · then, large: `WORDS HAVE WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a promise that trapped you. Sit and breathe. Think of a promise you made easily, that later got heavy. Maybe you're still keeping it. Maybe you broke it. Or think of a voice, like Manthara's, that talked you into something at night that looked different in the morning. No judgment. Just see the weight of the words. Then breathe out, and let them rest. The bell holds the time.
Vara, a boon once granted and almost forgotten, called in at last: Bharata to be crowned, and Rama sent into the forest for fourteen years.
Your line: words have weight. Today, before you promise anything, even something small, weigh it first. Day thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Hindus retell Kaikeyi's wishes as the turning point of the Ramayana; in Ramlila performances it's often the moment the audience goes quiet, and many discuss how much blame Kaikeyi and Manthara bear.

fork.setup: you're Dasharatha. your wife has made you swear on Rama's name, and now asks for his exile. what do you do?
options: break the promise; a son matters more.
keep your word, and beg her all night to change hers.
fork.reveal: he pleads and argues, but he can't take back a king's word. the promise holds, and it breaks him.

original.note: Sanskrit: a boon, a wish granted; also a choice, as in swayamvara.

trapdoor: what you thought: a jealous stepmother.
what it means: a frightened queen, a persuasive maid, and an old promise turned into a weapon.
what a scholar hears: vara, a boon, is the same word as the choosing in swayamvara; later tellings shift the blame toward the gods' plan through Saraswati.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 7–12 (Manthara; the anger chamber; the two boons)
Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kanda (Saraswati turns Manthara's mind)

notes: Boons granted when Kaikeyi saved Dasharatha in the war against Shambara (Ayodhya Kanda 9); confirm.
Kaikeyi's gift of an ornament to Manthara at the news: Ayodhya Kanda 7; confirm.
Saraswati sent by the gods to influence Manthara: in the Ramcharitmanas and Adhyatma Ramayana. Confirm attribution.
Rama's exile specifically to the Dandaka forest; simplified to 'the forest'.
